chapter_theme: The woman argues with her own heart about what to do: find a remedy, stop suffering, go to him, or forget him. The heart is a separate party that can be scolded, sent away and accused, and the chapter ends without any option having won.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's, addressed to her heart. Parimelazhagar finds a plot: she urges her heart to go to him (1242-1246), shame stops her (1247), she scolds the heart for going ahead (1248-1249), and she tells it to forget (1250). Manakkudavar reads the verses as independent utterances.

1241.reading: The woman asks her heart to think and tell her of some medicine, of whatever kind, for this incurable sickness.
1241.nuance: Parimelazhagar takes எனைத்தொன்றும், 'of any kind', very far: even a remedy that means giving up shame, which is dearer than life. The heart is asked because she herself no longer has the power to know.

1242.reading: The woman tells her heart, with a mocking blessing, that it's folly for it to suffer when he has no love.
1242.nuance: Parimelazhagar sees a surprising purpose in this: it isn't telling the heart to give up, but to stop waiting and go, since going would be wise. On this reading, it's the first move towards a woman going after a man.

1243.reading: The woman asks her heart why it sits and suffers, thinking of him, when the one who caused this sickness has no thought of pity.
1243.nuance: இருந்து, 'sitting here', is the barb, because the alternatives are stated in Parimelazhagar's gloss: neither going to him nor dying. Waiting has become the worst option.

1244.reading: The woman tells her heart to take the eyes with it if it goes, since they are eating her alive with longing to see him.
1244.nuance: A practical request and one of the book's most physical: the body has parts she wants to send away. By Parimelazhagar's reading, this is a way to mean that she herself will go, since she can't part with her eyes.

1245.reading: The woman asks her heart if one can really abandon him as an enemy, simply because he doesn't respond when she draws close.
1245.nuance: The commentators shift the emphasis subtly. For Parimelazhagar, she lacks the strength to abandon him; for Manakkudavar, the issue is whether it would be proper. One treats loyalty as weakness, and the other treats it as what's right.

1246.reading: The woman tells her heart that when it sees the man who ends quarrels by union, it can't stay angry, and so its present anger is false.
1246.nuance: She exposes her own anger as fake, calling it பொய்க்காய்வு. The heart is angry only while he's absent, and is no use when it would count.

1247.reading: The woman tells her good heart to give up either desire or shame, since she can't bear both.
1247.nuance: நன்னெஞ்சே, 'good heart', isn't flattery alone. For Parimelazhagar, the heart is good because holding on to both keeps her womanhood intact, but she can't afford that goodness, as her life is at stake. யானோ implies a split: 'you may be able to, I can't.'

1248.reading: The woman calls her heart a fool for following the man who has left, while lamenting that he isn't gracious.
1248.nuance: Parimelazhagar's surviving note gives the logic: he saw her distress and left anyway, so how would telling him at a distance change anything? This reverses 1242-1244, where she was urging the heart to go.

1249.reading: The woman asks her heart whom it goes looking for, since her lover is within it.
1249.nuance: Parimelazhagar says it's laughable to go looking outside for one who is inside. To me, this resembles the later devotional complaint about seeking God outside, though this resemblance isn't something the verse or its commentators claim.

1250.reading: The woman says that if she keeps in her heart the man who left without coming close, she will lose still more of her கவின்.

positions.position: She has lost her outward beauty, and will now lose her inner beauty too, meaning her dignity and restraint.
positions.quote: முன் இழந்த புறக்கவினேயன்றி நின்ற அகக்கவினும் இழப்போம்.

positions.position: It is bodily beauty that will fade further as she wastes away.

links.note: In 1163, love and shame hang in balance on the pole of her life, and she describes the strain. In 1247 she gives an ultimatum to drop one. Nothing has changed except that she can no longer carry them, and the next chapter tells us which goes.
In 1130 she uses 'he lives within me' to refute the town's gossip. In 1249 she uses the same fact against her own heart, to stop it from leaving. The argument that once consoled her now traps her.

In 1177 she curses her eyes to weep themselves dry. In 1244 they are eating her, and she wants them gone. The eyes haven't stopped, and her conflict with them has moved from revenge to getting rid of them.

source_issues: 1248: Parimelazhagar's entry is truncated. It starts at பின்செல்வாய் பேதையென் னெஞ்சு, so the headnote and gloss are missing.
1243: Pope's prose has 'lewd thoughts' where the Tamil and his own couplet concern pity.
1242: Manakkudavar has no aligned commentary. Parimelazhagar's gloss has அவா where அவர் seems intended.
